subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Attention as a Scarce Resource
description: One-minute skill: Attention as a Scarce Resource.

hook.text: A poker player watches six opponents, the pot, the cards, and a TV screen.

buildup.text: Attention is limited. In complex games, players can't track all relevant information, so they focus on salient cues.

discovery.text: Gabaix showed that limited attention explains pricing anomalies. If consumers can't process all product attributes.

twist.text: Strategic opponents can overload your attention deliberately. Complex contracts, long menus, and rapid decisions all.

climax.text: Simplify your decisions. When overwhelmed, focus on the 2 or 3 most important factors.

punchline.text: You cannot watch everything. Choose what to watch wisely.

quiz.question: How can opponents exploit limited attention?
options: By simplifying their strategies for transparency
By creating complexity that overloads decision-making
By reducing the number of choices available

details.summary: Behavioral game theory recognizes that players have limited attention, so they cannot process all available information. Strategic choices shift when players selectively focus on salient features rather than analyzing every possible outcome.
details.whyItMatters: Attention limits mean real strategic behavior departs from classical predictions. Designers of contracts, auctions, and policies must account for what people actually notice rather than what information is technically available.
takeaways: Players focus on salient features and ignore less prominent information
Limited attention changes which strategies people actually choose

faq.question: How does limited attention change game outcomes?
faq.answer: Players who miss key information make systematically different choices than fully informed players. This can shift equilibria, create exploitable blind spots, and make simple salient strategies dominate complex optimal ones.

faq.question: Can firms exploit consumers' limited attention?
faq.answer: Yes. Companies hide fees in fine print, emphasize attractive headline prices, and use complex pricing to exploit the fact that consumers cannot attend to everything. Regulation increasingly targets these attention-exploiting strategies.
